body.text: Two weeks after the German State of Saxony-Anhalt handed the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) its first single-largest-party status, the country went to the polls again on September 20 in the north-eastern State of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern and in the capital Berlin. Read separately, the results from these two areas might look like unrelated local stories. But read together, they describe a common underlying phenomenon from two opposite ends: the political centre in Germany is not just losing ground to the far-right wave; it is feeling the squeeze from both the Right and the Left.

In Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, the AfD bagged 32 of 71, falling just four short of an outright majority, and garnered 38.2 per cent of the vote, more than double its 2021 share. The incumbent Social Democratic Party (SPD) came second with 35.5 per cent, while Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s Christian Democratic Union (CDU) collapsed, winning just 4.9 per cent, below the 5 per cent threshold required to sit in parliament.
The CDU has never failed to reach the 5 per cent threshold in any State, European, or federal election. This is literally a new low for Merz and his party.

While the trend of the AfD’s rise continued in the north-eastern State, it inverted in Berlin. The Die Linke, also known as the Left Party, emerged as the winner with 25.7 per cent of the votes, its best Berlin result in decades, comfortably ahead of the runner-up CDU, which bagged 18.8 per cent, down from 28.2 per cent previously. The AfD, which came third, garnered 16.3 per cent, nearly doubling its 2023 vote share, while the SPD got just 12.1 per cent, its worst-ever showing in the capital.

It is tempting to put these State verdicts into two binaries. The Mecklenburg-Vorpommern verdict can be seen as furthering the AfD’s ascendancy journey from Saxony-Anhalt. In contrast, Berlin can be seen as Left consolidation holding the far right at bay.

But this temptation misses a crucial structural point: that on a single Sunday, two different parts of Germany abandoned the CDU and the SPD to favour the parties that sit further from the centre, one on the Right and another on the Left.
One story from two directions

This is a story about the crumbling of the country’s traditional Volksparteien, the broad-tent parties that have led the country, anchoring governing coalitions since the 1950s. These are not two separate stories running in parallel but a singular story being told from two directions at once.

Chancellor Merz and his CDU are feeling this squeeze the most. Across three State elections held within a short period, the CDU has produced three of its weakest results: Saxony-Anhalt at 17.2 per cent, Mecklenburg-Vorpommern at 4.9 per cent with zero seats, and Berlin at 18.8 per cent.

Just minutes after the first projections were released, Merz called the results in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern “a disaster” but struck a defiant note, stating that moving forward would require backbone, resolve, and patience and that he would muster them “as chairman of the CDU and, above all, as the chancellor of our country”.

While defiance, at face value, might look good, what matters now is what is being discussed in the backrooms. For a party, failing to clear the threshold for the first time in its history is a more important data point than another strong AfD performance.

The question now is not whether the AfD will keep gaining but whether Merz himself will survive a streak of bad results without a serious internal challenge, from the party and from the governing coalition at the centre, as the speculation about a replacement that began after Saxony-Anhalt is about to grow louder.

The electoral story in Saxony-Anhalt was substantially an east-west divide, driven by economic divide and the issue of immigration. The AfD found its strength primarily in the former East, with less exposure to migration than in the West but a deeper demographic and economic divide since unification. Berlin complicates this framing because it also sits in the former East but has produced an opposing result.

This suggests that east-west may not be the only axis worth analysing here. A plausible reading of what separates Mecklenburg-Vorpommern and Berlin is not limited to an east-versus-west binary. It may have more to do with a rural, ageing, economically stagnant populace versus a young, educated one. Based on this reading, the AfD gains in small towns and the countryside, while a party like the Left gains in exactly Berlin-like urban, university-adjacent, rent-heavy constituencies.
Housing a major campaign issue in Berlin

A survey conducted by Infratest dimap BerlinTrend found that 30 per cent of Berliners named housing/rent as the single most important issue in the campaign. This housing anxiety also appears real, with reports suggesting that Berlin will need more than 200,000 additional homes by 2040 and that advertised rents have nearly doubled since 2014.

This does not prove that the Left party’s surge was due to the housing crisis and not an anti-AfD reflex. The surveys only show that housing topped voters’ minds, not necessarily party choice. This does not disprove the idea that Berlin’s result could have been an anti-AfD backlash, but it does suggest that understanding it as anti-AfD is not the whole story.

It does raise a genuine possibility, though perhaps unproven, that Germany’s political map may have started to fracture along two axes at once: east-west and urban-rural, with the CDU and the SPD losing ground on both.

Perhaps the most immediate practical consequence of State results is that coalition arithmetic is getting harder everywhere, not just in AfD strongholds. For example, in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, the SPD and the Left together account for 34 of the 71 seats, two short of a majority, which means they would need a tripartite arrangement, probably with the Greens, an environmentalist political party.

In Berlin, only a three-party coalition will command a comfortable majority without including either Die Linke or the AfD. Germany has exclusively witnessed two-party coalitions at the federal level from 1949 until 2021, when the three-party “traffic light” coalition of the SPD, the Greens, and the Free Democratic Party (FDP) came together to form the country’s first three-party federal government, which eventually collapsed within three years.

The recent State elections suggest that the older formula of one dominant party plus a single hinge partner may soon become an exception rather than the norm. Stable majorities would increasingly require either working with flank parties, once considered unthinkable, or cobbling together a three- or four-party coalition held together by necessity, excluding whichever party they find least acceptable rather than based on mutual ideals.

In this arithmetic, a question for the German mainstream lies unanswered. Merz’s CDU has posted historic lows in two States and has failed to clear the threshold in one. AfD leaders are framing it as a supplanting of the party as Germany’s mainstream force on the Right.

There will come a time when the arithmetic may simply stop leaving the CDU a path back to power without aligning with the far right or the far left. Now, whether that point arrives before or after the CDU’s own instinct for survival overtakes its long-held commitment to the “Brandmauer”(firewall) policy of preventing the rise of the far right remains to be seen. But, for now, it is a fair question to ask.

Ashutosh Nagda is a Senior Researcher with the Institute of Peace and Conflict Studies (IPCS), New Delhi. He is a former German Chancellor Fellow (2023-24) and regularly writes on Germany and India’s foreign policy and domestic politics.
